Purpose is to provide an inkjet recording method for forming high-quality color image on a thick recording medium having low thermal conductance rate. The present invention is a single-pass inkjet recording method using an ink set including at least two active ray-curing color inks, and a recording medium having thermal conductivity of less than 0.10 W/(m·K) and thickness of 0.4 mm or more. The ink set containing two color inks satisfy only condition (a), and the ink set containing three or more color inks satisfy conditions (a) and (b): (a) most downstream color ink has a gelation temperature which is 3.0° C. to 15.0° C. higher than that of most upstream color ink, and (b) second or subsequent color ink from the most upstream position in conveyance direction has a gelation temperature which is the same as or higher than that of an adjacent color ink at the upstream position.

The purpose of the present invention is to provide an inkjet recording method for forming a high-quality color image on a thick recording medium having low thermal conductivity. The invention provides a single-pass inkjet recording method that uses an ink set comprising at least two active-ray-curable color inks and a recording medium having a thermal conductivity of less than 0.10 W/(m·K) and a thickness of 0.4 mm or greater. An ink set comprising two color inks satisfies condition (a) below, while an ink set comprising three or more color inks satisfies both conditions (a) and (b):

(a) The most downstream color ink has a gelation temperature that is 3.0°C to 15.0°C higher than that of the most upstream color ink; and

(b) Each color ink positioned second or later from the most upstream position in the conveyance direction has a gelation temperature equal to or higher than that of the adjacent color ink positioned immediately upstream.

The objective is to produce high-quality color images by inkjet printing on a thick recording substrate with low thermal conductivity. The invention provides a single-pass inkjet recording process that uses an ink set containing at least two color inks curable by active rays. The recording medium has a thermal conductivity below 0.10 W/(m·K) and a thickness of at least 0.4 mm.

For an ink set comprising two color inks, only requirement (a) must be met. For a set comprising three or more color inks, both requirements (a) and (b) apply:

(a) The color ink positioned farthest downstream has a gelation temperature 3.0°C to 15.0°C above that of the color ink positioned farthest upstream.

(b) Starting with the second color ink from the upstream end in the conveyance direction, each color ink has a gelation temperature equal to or greater than that of the immediately adjacent ink on its upstream side.
outputs.L3:
This method is designed to form high-quality color images on thick recording media with low thermal conductivity. It employs a single-pass inkjet process using at least two active ray-curable color inks. The recording medium has a thermal conductivity of less than 0.10 W/(m·K) and a thickness of at least 0.4 mm.

When a two-color ink set is used, the gelation temperature of the most downstream ink must be 3.0°C to 15.0°C higher than that of the most upstream ink. When the ink set contains three or more colors, each downstream ink must have a gelation temperature equal to or higher than that of the adjacent upstream ink. This controlled gelation-temperature relationship supports stable ink deposition and helps produce high-quality color images on thermally insulating, relatively thick media.
outputs.L4:
A single-pass inkjet recording method is provided for producing high-quality color images on recording media having relatively low thermal conductivity and a thickness of at least 0.4 mm. The method uses two or more color inks that are curable by irradiation with an active ray, such as ultraviolet radiation. Each ink contains a gelling component and is formulated to undergo a sol–gel phase transition at a controlled gelation temperature.

During recording, the medium is conveyed once past a plurality of inkjet recording heads arranged along the transport direction. The heads eject the different color inks in sequence to form a multicolor image, after which the deposited inks are irradiated with the active ray and cured. Because thick, low-thermal-conductivity media respond differently to heat and retain temperature locally, uncontrolled gelation can allow previously deposited droplets to spread, mix with subsequently deposited inks, or develop uneven gloss and density.

To suppress these defects, the gelation temperature of the ink ejected from the most downstream recording head is set higher than that of the ink ejected from the most upstream recording head. The difference between these gelation temperatures is maintained within a range of 3°C to 15°C. When three or more color inks are used, the inks are preferably arranged so that their gelation temperatures do not decrease from the upstream side toward the downstream side of the recording-head array.

This temperature relationship controls the spreading and immobilization of droplets throughout the sequential deposition process. It reduces intercolor bleeding, coalescence, density irregularities, and other image defects while promoting uniform dot formation and stable curing. As a result, sharp, high-quality color images can be formed reliably in a single pass even on thick recording media with low thermal conductivity.

## The Purpose

Purpose gives direction to our lives. It is the reason behind our choices, efforts, and dreams. For some people, purpose comes from their work; for others, it is found in relationships, creativity, service, or personal growth. It does not always appear as one great calling. Often, it develops gradually through everyday experiences.

Having a purpose does not mean knowing exactly where life will lead. Instead, it provides a sense of meaning that helps us move forward, especially during difficult times. Purpose encourages us to look beyond immediate success and consider how our actions affect other people and the world around us.

Ultimately, purpose is deeply personal. It can change as we learn, grow, and face new circumstances. The important thing is not to discover a perfect answer, but to live with intention and remain open to what gives life genuine meaning.

counterfactuals.prompt: What is the disclosed invention for producing high-quality color images on a recording medium with thermal conductivity below 0.10 W/(m·K) and thickness of at least 0.4 mm?
counterfactuals.output:
The disclosed invention is an **inkjet color-recording method for thick, heat-insulating media**, such as cardboard or similar substrates having thermal conductivity under 0.10 W/(m·K) and thickness of 0.4 mm or more.  

It controls the medium’s surface temperature—by heating the recording surface—and then deposits the different colored inks in a controlled sequence, followed by drying/fixing. This promotes rapid immobilization of the ink at the surface, suppressing bleeding and color mixing so that sharp, high-density color images can be obtained even though heat does not readily pass through the medium.

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a concise patent-style abstract for an inkjet recording method using active ray-curing color inks, including conditions (a) and (b) for ink gelation temperatures.
counterfactuals.output: An inkjet recording method comprises heating two or more active ray-curable color inks to a sol state, ejecting the inks onto a recording medium, cooling the deposited inks to induce gelation, and irradiating the gelled inks with active rays to cure an image. The inks satisfy: (a) each ink has a gelation temperature of 40–90°C; and (b) the difference between the highest and lowest gelation temperatures is 10°C or less. The method suppresses intercolor bleeding and produces high-definition, uniformly cured images.
